claim: People make about three ballistic eye movements (saccades) per second orienting the central part of the vision (the fovea) to regions of interest in the world and acquiring high-acuity visual information.
source: People make about three ballistic eye movements (saccades) per second orienting the central part of the vision (the fovea) to regions of interest in the world and acquiring high-acuity visual information (Bahill et al., 1975).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bahill et al., 1975

claim: A foveated visual system allocates more retinal cells to the central part of the visual field.
source: A foveated visual system allocates more retinal cells (Curcio et al., 1987), thalamic, cortical (Azzopardi and Cowey, 1993), and superior colliculus (Chen et al., 2019) neurons to the central part of the visual field and allows for computational and metabolic savings.
evidence: Supported by citation to Curcio et al., 1987

claim: A foveated visual system allocates more thalamic and cortical neurons to the central part of the visual field.
source: A foveated visual system allocates more retinal cells (Curcio et al., 1987), thalamic, cortical (Azzopardi and Cowey, 1993), and superior colliculus (Chen et al., 2019) neurons to the central part of the visual field and allows for computational and metabolic savings.
evidence: Supported by citation to Azzopardi and Cowey, 1993

claim: A foveated visual system allocates more superior colliculus neurons to the central part of the visual field.
source: A foveated visual system allocates more retinal cells (Curcio et al., 1987), thalamic, cortical (Azzopardi and Cowey, 1993), and superior colliculus (Chen et al., 2019) neurons to the central part of the visual field and allows for computational and metabolic savings.
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2019

claim: A foveated visual system allows for computational and metabolic savings.
source: A foveated visual system allocates more retinal cells (Curcio et al., 1987), thalamic, cortical (Azzopardi and Cowey, 1993), and superior colliculus (Chen et al., 2019) neurons to the central part of the visual field and allows for computational and metabolic savings.
evidence: Based on knowledge about the efficiency of foveated vision systems

claim: Gaze-following behavior can be observed as early as 8–10 months in infants.
source: Gaze-following behavior can be observed as early as 8–10 months in infants and is widely found in nonhumans such as macaques, dogs, and goats (Brooks and Meltzoff, 2005; Kaminski et al., 2005; Senju and Csibra, 2008; Shepherd, 2010; Wallis et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brooks and Meltzoff, 2005; Kaminski et al., 2005; Senju and Csibra, 2008; Shepherd, 2010; Wallis et al., 2015

claim: Gaze-following behavior is widely found in nonhumans such as macaques, dogs, and goats.
source: Gaze-following behavior can be observed as early as 8–10 months in infants and is widely found in nonhumans such as macaques, dogs, and goats (Brooks and Meltzoff, 2005; Kaminski et al., 2005; Senju and Csibra, 2008; Shepherd, 2010; Wallis et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brooks and Meltzoff, 2005; Kaminski et al., 2005; Senju and Csibra, 2008; Shepherd, 2010; Wallis et al., 2015

claim: The presence of a person at the gaze goal reduces the angular error of the first saccade.
source: We found a significant main effect of the presence of a person at the gaze goal location for saccade angular error (2 (present or absent) x 2 (target or distractor) ANOVA, F(1,24) = 100, p = 4.85e-10, η2 = 0.987, Figure 2e). The angular error was higher when the person at the gaze goal was absent target: 57.4 degrees for absent vs. 32.8 degrees for present; distractor: 54.9 degrees for absent vs. 29.3 degrees for present.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) and data shown in Figure 2e

claim: The presence of a person at the gaze goal reduces the amplitude error of the first saccade.
source: We also found that the presence of a person at the gaze goal in the periphery reduced the amplitude error (Figure 2e, 2 (present or absent) x 2 (target or distractor) ANOVA, F(1,24)=207, p = 2.7e-13, η2 = 0.99). The amplitude error was higher when a person was absent vs. present for both target (Figure 2e, absent 4.23° vs. present 1.87°, p = 3.27e-119 with FDR) and distractor (absent 4.43° vs. present 1.98°, p = 1.1e-144 with FDR).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) and data shown in Figure 2e

claim: The presence of a person at the gaze goal reduces the Euclidean error of the first saccade.
source: It also reduced the Euclidean error that combines the angular and amplitude error (2 (present or absent) x 2 (target or distractor) ANOVA, F(1,24)=259, p = 2.3e-14, η2 = 0.99). The Euclidean error was higher when the target was absent vs. preent (Figure 2e, absent 5.08° vs. present 2.50°, p = 1.4e-91, with FDR) and the same of the distractor (absent 5.25° vs. present 2.60°, p = 6.8e-106, with FDR).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) and data shown in Figure 2e

claim: The presence of a person at the gaze goal reduces the first saccade latency.
source: The presence of a person at the gaze goal also impacts the first saccade latency, (F(1,24)=50.5, p = 2.4e-07, η2 = 0.97). The saccade latency was significantly higher (Figure 2f) when a person was absent vs. present at the gaze goal for both target (0.37 s vs. 0.31 s, p = 1.4e-16) and distractor (0.38 s vs. 0.31 s, p = 2.0e-19) trials.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) and data shown in Figure 2f

claim: Observers make anticipatory first saccades that infer the direction of the gaze goal beyond the momentary information from the gazer's head direction.
source: The findings suggest that observers make anticipatory first saccades that infer the direction of the gaze goal beyond the momentary information from the gazer's head direction.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that mean angular error for saccade directions was significantly smaller than that of the gazer vector at the time of saccade initiation (18 degrees vs. 40 degrees, bootstrap p<1e-4, Cohen's d=0.71)

claim: The mean angular error for the saccade directions was significantly smaller than that of the gazer vector at the time of saccade initiation.
source: The mean angular error for the saccade directions was significantly smaller than that of the gazer vector at the time of saccade initiation (18 degrees vs. 40 degrees, bootstrap p<1e-4, Cohen's d=0.71).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis using bootstrap test

claim: On average it took 0.37 s for the gaze vector to reach the saccade vector direction for videos with target/distractor-present.
source: On average it took 0.37 s (std across observers = 0.09 s) and 0.22 s (std across observers = 0.09 s) for the gaze vector to reach the saccade vector direction for videos with target/distractor-present and target/distractor-absent respectively.
evidence: Calculated from the data comparing saccade direction and gazer head direction over time

claim: On average it took 0.22 s for the gaze vector to reach the saccade vector direction for videos with target/distractor-absent.
source: On average it took 0.37 s (std across observers = 0.09 s) and 0.22 s (std across observers = 0.09 s) for the gaze vector to reach the saccade vector direction for videos with target/distractor-present and target/distractor-absent respectively.
evidence: Calculated from the data comparing saccade direction and gazer head direction over time

claim: Participants executed backward saccades in the opposite direction of the gazer vector (reverse saccades) in 22% of all trials.
source: Even if we explicitly instructed participants to follow the gaze, our analysis of eye position revealed that participants executed backward saccades in the opposite direction of the gazer vector (reverse saccades) in 22% of all trials (see Figure 4a , demo video Video 1).
evidence: Supported by data analysis and shown in Figure 4a

claim: The mean reverse saccade initiation time was 0.63 s.
source: The mean reverse saccade initiation time was 0.63 s (std = 0.07 s, Figure 4b) with a mean amplitude of 3.5° (std = 1.2°).
evidence: Supported by data analysis and shown in Figure 4b

claim: The mean amplitude of reverse saccades was 3.5°.
source: The mean reverse saccade initiation time was 0.63 s (std = 0.07 s, Figure 4b) with a mean amplitude of 3.5° (std = 1.2°).
evidence: Supported by data analysis and shown in Figure 4b

claim: Over 80% of the reverse saccades were either the second or the third saccade in the trial.
source: Over 80% of the reverse saccades were either the second or the third saccade in the trial (reverse saccade index, Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by data analysis and shown in Figure 4b

claim: Trials with reverse saccade had significantly shorter first saccade latencies compared to those without reverse saccade.
source: Trials with reverse saccade had significantly shorter first saccade latencies compared to those without reverse saccade (F(1,24)=96.8, p = 6.8e-10, η2 = 0.84, Figure 4d, target/distractor-present condition 0.23 s vs. 0.34 s, p=2.6e-67, absent condition 0.27 s vs. 0.40 s, p=4.2e-50, both posthoc pairwise comparison with FDR).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) and data shown in Figure 4d

claim: Trials with reverse saccades had significantly lower head velocity during the first 0.23 s of the video compared to trials without reverse saccades.
source: Instead, we found a significantly lower head velocity during the first 0.23 s of the video for the trials with reverse saccades, 63.6 degrees/s vs. 93.6 degrees/s, cluster-based permutation test, p=1.0e-04, Cohen's d=1.9 (Figure 4e, average head velocity lined up with video start).
evidence: Supported by cluster-based permutation test and data shown in Figure 4e

claim: When the gazer's head velocity is slow, observers make an inference that the gazer might be stopping her or his head movement.
source: These findings suggest that when the gazer's head velocity is slow, observers make an inference that the gazer might be stopping her or his head movement.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that trials with reverse saccades had significantly lower head velocity during the first 0.23 s of the video

claim: Head velocity had the highest accuracy in predicting reverse saccade movies among all gaze features.
source: We found that the head velocity had the highest accuracy in predicting reverse saccade movies among all gaze features. The model's accuracy peaked when we used head velocity information from 0 to 230ms of each video (71.2%) and asymptoted afterward.
evidence: Supported by SVM model analysis comparing different gaze features

claim: Freezing the video frame after the first saccade execution did not reduce the proportion of trials with reverse saccade relative to the unfrozen videos trials.
source: However, we found that freezing the video frame after the first saccade execution did not reduce the proportion of trials with reverse saccade relative to the unfrozen videos trials, (mean = 22%, std = 12% for frozen vs. mean = 21%, std = 11% for unfrozen, bootstrap p=0.6).
evidence: Supported by experimental manipulation and statistical analysis using bootstrap test

claim: Observers planned the reverse saccade prior to the execution of the first forward saccade.
source: These results suggest that observers planned the reverse saccade prior to the execution of the first forward saccade.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that freezing the video frame after the first saccade execution did not reduce the proportion of trials with reverse saccade

claim: The reverse saccades landed close to the gazer's head with a mean distance of 0.79°.
source: We found that the reverse saccades landed close to the gazer's head (Figure 5a; mean distance to the gazer's head 0.79°, std = 0.28°) suggesting that the reverse saccades aim to re-fixate the gazer given the change in the gazer vector after execution of the first saccade.
evidence: Supported by data analysis and shown in Figure 5a

claim: Saccade angular error was lower following the reverse saccades for the target/distractor-present condition.
source: We found that saccade angular error was lower following the reverse saccades for both the target/distractor-present condition (Figure 5c, 20.53 degrees for post-reverse saccade vs. 33.7 degrees for pre-reverse, bootstrap p=0.0014, Cohen's d=0.44, corrected by FDR) and for the target/distractor-absent condition (34.37 degrees for post-reverse saccade vs. 71.01 degrees for pre-reverse, bootstrap p<1e-4, Cohen's d=1.2, corrected by FDR).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis using bootstrap test and data shown in Figure 5c

claim: Saccade angular error was lower following the reverse saccades for the target/distractor-absent condition.
source: We found that saccade angular error was lower following the reverse saccades for both the target/distractor-present condition (Figure 5c, 20.53 degrees for post-reverse saccade vs. 33.7 degrees for pre-reverse, bootstrap p=0.0014, Cohen's d=0.44, corrected by FDR) and for the target/distractor-absent condition (34.37 degrees for post-reverse saccade vs. 71.01 degrees for pre-reverse, bootstrap p<1e-4, Cohen's d=1.2, corrected by FDR).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis using bootstrap test and data shown in Figure 5c

claim: The saccade amplitude error was lower following reverse saccades for the target/distractor-present condition.
source: The saccade amplitude error was lower following reverse saccades (Figure 5d; pre-reverse saccade1.6° vs. post-reverse saccade 1.3°, p=0.017, Cohen's d=0.38, based on bootstrap resampling, see methods).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis using bootstrap test and data shown in Figure 5d

claim: Forward saccades following a reverse saccade ended closer to the gaze goal than the saccades before reverse saccades.
source: Overall, forward saccades following a reverse saccade ended closer to the gaze goal than the saccades before reverse saccades (Euclidean error, Figure 5e; 1.8° for post-reverse saccade vs. 2.5° for pre-reverse, p=0.0054, Cohen's d=0.5).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 5e

claim: The saccade angular error post-reverse saccade was significantly higher in the trials with the gazer removed compared to those with unaltered videos for the target/distractor-present condition.
source: Critical to our hypotheses of interest, the results showed that the saccade angular error post-reverse saccade was significantly higher in the trials with the gazer removed compared to those with unaltered videos, for both the target/distractor-present condition (28.2 degrees pre-reverse saccade vs. 9.2 degrees, post-reverse saccade, bootstrap p<1e-4, Cohen's d=1.05) and absent conditions (46.0 degrees pre-reverse saccade vs. 12.8 degrees post-reverse saccade, bootstrap p=1e-4, Cohen's d=1.06, Figure 6c).
evidence: Supported by experimental manipulation and statistical analysis using bootstrap test, data shown in Figure 6c

claim: The saccade angular error post-reverse saccade was significantly higher in the trials with the gazer removed compared to those with unaltered videos for the target/distractor-absent condition.
source: Critical to our hypotheses of interest, the results showed that the saccade angular error post-reverse saccade was significantly higher in the trials with the gazer removed compared to those with unaltered videos, for both the target/distractor-present condition (28.2 degrees pre-reverse saccade vs. 9.2 degrees, post-reverse saccade, bootstrap p<1e-4, Cohen's d=1.05) and absent conditions (46.0 degrees pre-reverse saccade vs. 12.8 degrees post-reverse saccade, bootstrap p=1e-4, Cohen's d=1.06, Figure 6c).
evidence: Supported by experimental manipulation and statistical analysis using bootstrap test, data shown in Figure 6c

claim: The benefit of reducing the gaze-following saccade errors is causally linked to the uptake of additional gaze goal information from re-fixating the gazer with a reverse saccade.
source: This finding confirms that the benefit of reducing the gaze-following saccade errors is causally linked to the uptake of additional gaze goal information from re-fixating the gazer with a reverse saccade.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental manipulation showing that removing the gazer increased saccade errors post-reverse saccade

claim: Participants spontaneously executed gaze-following saccades for 74% of the trials for the absent condition in the free-viewing search experiment.
source: We found that participants spontaneously executed gaze-following saccades for 74% (std = 10%) and 91% (std=7.4%) of the trials for the absent and the present condition, respectively (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data analysis in Experiment 3 and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: Participants spontaneously executed gaze-following saccades for 91% of the trials for the present condition in the free-viewing search experiment.
source: We found that participants spontaneously executed gaze-following saccades for 74% (std = 10%) and 91% (std=7.4%) of the trials for the absent and the present condition, respectively (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data analysis in Experiment 3 and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: Observers executed anticipatory first saccades prior to the end of the gazer's head movement in 88% of the trials in the free-viewing search experiment.
source: Observers also executed anticipatory first saccades prior to the end of the gazer's head movement in 88% of the trials.
evidence: Supported by data analysis in Experiment 3

claim: Observers executed reverse saccades in 33% of trials for the absent condition in the free-viewing search experiment.
source: We also observed an even larger number of reverse saccades than in the first experiment where observers were instructed to follow the gazer (33%, std = 22% and 37%, std = 16%) of trials for the absent and the target or distractor present condition, respectively.
evidence: Supported by data analysis in Experiment 3

claim: Observers executed reverse saccades in 37% of trials for the target or distractor present condition in the free-viewing search experiment.
source: We also observed an even larger number of reverse saccades than in the first experiment where observers were instructed to follow the gazer (33%, std = 22% and 37%, std = 16%) of trials for the absent and the target or distractor present condition, respectively.
evidence: Supported by data analysis in Experiment 3

claim: Anticipatory and reverse saccades are not a byproduct of the instructions in experiment 1.
source: These findings suggest that anticipatory and reverse saccades are not a byproduct of the instructions in experiment 1.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that anticipatory and reverse saccades occurred in Experiment 3 where observers were not instructed to follow the gazer

claim: The oculomotor system integrates information about the foveally presented gazer's head and peripheral information about potential gaze goals.
source: First, we found that the oculomotor system integrates information about the foveally presented gazer's head and peripheral information about potential gaze goals.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that the presence of gaze goals reduced saccade errors and latencies

claim: The brain uses peripheral information to make an active prediction about likely gaze goals.
source: This suggests that the brain is using peripheral information to make an active prediction about likely gaze goals.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that first saccades contain information about the direction of the gaze goal that is more accurate than the direction information provided by the gazer's head at the time of saccade initiation

claim: The first saccades were anticipating the head direction by 340–370ms for target present conditions.
source: We found that on average the first saccades were anticipating the head direction by 340–370ms and 160–220ms for target present and absent conditions.
evidence: Calculated from the data comparing saccade timing and gazer head direction timing

claim: The first saccades were anticipating the head direction by 160–220ms for target absent conditions.
source: We found that on average the first saccades were anticipating the head direction by 340–370ms and 160–220ms for target present and absent conditions.
evidence: Calculated from the data comparing saccade timing and gazer head direction timing

claim: A saccade is typically based on visual information presented ~100ms before saccade execution.
source: Furthermore, previous studies have shown that a saccade is typically based on visual information presented ~100ms before saccade execution (Becker and Jürgens, 1979; Caspi et al., 2004; Hooge and Erkelens, 1999; Ludwig et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Becker and Jürgens, 1979; Caspi et al., 2004; Hooge and Erkelens, 1999; Ludwig et al., 2005

claim: The observers' first saccades might be anticipating the gazer's head direction by 440–470ms for target present conditions.
source: Thus, the first saccade might only have access to the gazer's head direction up to ~100ms before saccade execution, which means the observes' first saccades might be anticipating the gazer's head direction by 440–470ms and 260–320ms.
evidence: Calculated by adding the 100ms saccade programming delay to the 340-370ms anticipation time

claim: The observers' first saccades might be anticipating the gazer's head direction by 260–320ms for target absent conditions.
source: Thus, the first saccade might only have access to the gazer's head direction up to ~100ms before saccade execution, which means the observes' first saccades might be anticipating the gazer's head direction by 440–470ms and 260–320ms.
evidence: Calculated by adding the 100ms saccade programming delay to the 160-220ms anticipation time

claim: The gazer's head direction at the time of saccade programming was, on average, pointing 44.1 degrees away from the gaze goal for target/distractor present trials.
source: Similarly, the gazer's head direction at the time of saccade programming (rather than execution) was, on average, pointing 44.1 degrees (for target/distractor present trials) and 39.7 degrees (for target/distractor absent trials) away from the gaze goal.
evidence: Calculated from the data comparing gazer head direction and gaze goal direction at the time of saccade programming

claim: The gazer's head direction at the time of saccade programming was, on average, pointing 39.7 degrees away from the gaze goal for target/distractor absent trials.
source: Similarly, the gazer's head direction at the time of saccade programming (rather than execution) was, on average, pointing 44.1 degrees (for target/distractor present trials) and 39.7 degrees (for target/distractor absent trials) away from the gaze goal.
evidence: Calculated from the data comparing gazer head direction and gaze goal direction at the time of saccade programming

claim: The observers' oculomotor system might use multiple cues (head velocity, head deceleration, estimated gaze errors, etc) to infer that the gazer's head might stop and trigger gaze-following saccades.
source: Thus, we suggest that the observers' oculomotor system might use multiple cues (head velocity, head deceleration, estimated gaze errors, etc) to infer that the gazer's head might stop and trigger gaze-following saccades.
evidence: Inferred from the analysis of head velocity and deceleration patterns before saccade execution

claim: There is a 50–100ms delay between the programming of a saccade and its execution.
source: Studies have shown that there is a 50–100ms delay between the programming of a saccade and its execution (Becker and Jürgens, 1979; Caspi et al., 2004; Ludwig et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Becker and Jürgens, 1979; Caspi et al., 2004; Ludwig et al., 2005

claim: The concurrent programming of saccades has been documented for simplified lab experiments.
source: This concurrent programming of saccades has been documented for simplified lab experiments (Becker and Jürgens, 1979; Caspi et al., 2004) but not in the context of real-world stimuli and tasks.
evidence: Supported by citations to Becker and Jürgens, 1979; Caspi et al., 2004

claim: In 15% of reverse saccade trials, first saccades landed within 0.5° visual angle of the target but were still followed by reverse saccades.
source: In a small percentage of trials (15% of reverse saccade trials) first saccades landed within 0.5° visual angle of the target but these were still followed by reverse saccades.
evidence: Supported by data analysis

claim: Humans make reverse saccades in other visual tasks that require maintaining information in working memory, such as copying a color block pattern across two locations.
source: Are the reverse saccades unique to gaze following? No, humans make reverse saccades in other visual tasks that require maintaining information in working memory, such as copying a color block pattern across two locations (Hayhoe and Ballard, 2005; Hayhoe, 2017; Meghanathan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hayhoe and Ballard, 2005; Hayhoe, 2017; Meghanathan et al., 2019

claim: Regressive saccades during reading are related to inaccurate eye movements that missed critical words or fixations that are too short to deeply process a word's meaning.
source: Regressive saccades during reading are related to inaccurate eye movements that missed critical words or fixations that are too short to deeply process a word's meaning (Inhoff et al., 2019; Rayner, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Inhoff et al., 2019; Rayner, 1998

claim: The reverse saccades while following dynamic gaze are related to moment-to-moment changes in the visual information in the world (i.e. the gazer's head velocity) and the oculomotor systems' rapid response to optimize gaze-following.
source: The reverse saccades while following dynamic gaze are related to moment-to-moment changes in the visual information in the world (i.e. the gazer's head velocity) and the oculomotor systems' rapid response to optimize gaze-following.
evidence: Inferred from the findings that reverse saccades are triggered by low head velocity and improve subsequent saccade accuracy

claim: Gaze position is related to neuronal response properties in the superior temporal sulcus.
source: There is a large literature relating gaze position to neuronal response properties in the superior temporal sulcus (Oram and Perrett, 1994) and dorsal prefrontal cortex (Lanzilotto et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oram and Perrett, 1994

claim: Gaze position is related to neuronal response properties in the dorsal prefrontal cortex.
source: There is a large literature relating gaze position to neuronal response properties in the superior temporal sulcus (Oram and Perrett, 1994) and dorsal prefrontal cortex (Lanzilotto et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lanzilotto et al., 2017

claim: The concurrent programming of saccades has been related to neurons in the Frontal Eye Fields (FEF).
source: Finally, the concurrent programming of saccades has been related to neurons in the Frontal Eye Fields (FEF, Basu and Murthy, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Basu and Murthy, 2020

claim: The mean angle subtended by the heads in the videos was 1.47°.
source: The mean angle subtended by the heads in our videos (1.47°, std = 0.32°) would match the angle subtended by a real-sized head viewed at a distance of 9.3 m (std = 2.0 m) in real life.
evidence: Calculated from the video stimuli properties

claim: The mean angle subtended by the heads in the videos would match the angle subtended by a real-sized head viewed at a distance of 9.3 m in real life.
source: The mean angle subtended by the heads in our videos (1.47°, std = 0.32°) would match the angle subtended by a real-sized head viewed at a distance of 9.3 m (std = 2.0 m) in real life.
evidence: Calculated based on the visual angle and typical head size

claim: At a distance of 9.3 m, the eye subtends a mean angle of 0.147° (vertically).
source: At that distance, the eye subtends a mean angle of 0.147° (vertically) providing a poor source of information to infer the gaze goals compared to the head orientation.
evidence: Calculated based on the distance and typical eye size

claim: Twenty-five observers viewed 80 in-house videos (1.2 s long) of an actor (gazer) actively shifting his/her head and gaze to look at another person (gaze goal) in the video.
source: Twenty-five observers viewed 80 in-house videos (1.2 s long, different settings) of an actor (gazer) actively shifting his/her head and gaze to look at another person (gaze goal) in the video.
evidence: Description of the experimental design

claim: In 25% of the videos, the target person was present and always the gaze goal.
source: In 25% of the videos, the target person was present and always the gaze goal (Figure 1b).
evidence: Description of the experimental design shown in Figure 1b

claim: In 25% of the videos, a distractor person was the gaze goal and the target person was absent.
source: In another 25%, a distractor person (Figure 1c) was the gaze goal and the target person was absent.
evidence: Description of the experimental design shown in Figure 1c

claim: In 50% of the videos, no person was at the gazed location.
source: In the remaining 50%, no person was at the gazed location (d-e).
evidence: Description of the experimental design shown in Figure 1d-e

claim: Observers typically executed 3–5 saccades per trial.
source: Observers typically executed 3–5 saccades. Figure 1f shows a histogram of the number of executed saccades per trial.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1f

claim: The gazers' head movements started with the video onset and their mean duration was 0.61 s.
source: The gazers' head movements started with the video onset and their mean duration was 0.61 s.
evidence: Calculated from the video stimuli

claim: The observers' mean first saccade latency was 0.34 s.
source: The observers' mean first saccade latency was 0.34 s (std = 0.07 s).
evidence: Calculated from the eye movement data

claim: In 81% of the trials, participants initiated the first saccade before the gazer's head movement stopped.
source: In 81% of the trials, participants initiated the first saccade before the gazer's head movement stopped (86% of the trials for target-present, 85% for distractor-present, and 77% for target/distractor-absent trials).
evidence: Calculated from the eye movement data

claim: The accuracy of the DNN model in estimating the gaze goal location for these images is comparable to that of humans for target/distractor present trials.
source: The accuracy of the DNN model in estimating the gaze goal location for these images is comparable to that of humans for target/distractor present and superior to humans for target/distractor-absent trials (Han and Eckstein, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Han and Eckstein, 2022

claim: The accuracy of the DNN model in estimating the gaze goal location for these images is superior to humans for target/distractor-absent trials.
source: The accuracy of the DNN model in estimating the gaze goal location for these images is comparable to that of humans for target/distractor present and superior to humans for target/distractor-absent trials (Han and Eckstein, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Han and Eckstein, 2022

claim: In 87% of the videos, the gazer started to look away from the gazer person at the end of the movie.
source: In 87% of the videos, the gazer started to look away from the gazer person at the end of the movie (DNN estimation mean = 0.98 s, std = 0.18 s, human estimation mean = 1.06 s, std = 0.15 s).
evidence: Calculated from the video stimuli using DNN and human estimation

claim: The majority of reverse saccades (88%) were executed before the gazer started looking away.
source: In those videos, the majority of reverse saccades (88%) were executed before the gazer started looking away.
